# Issues

**The register of everything open in this repo.** Defects, gaps, and questions
awaiting a ruling. One id per item, stable forever.

**This file is the source of truth for what is open.** Nothing is open unless it
is here. Other documents no longer carry their own open-item lists — they link
here. Long analysis may stay where it was argued (`packages/*/PROJECT_STATE.md`,
`IDEAS/*.md`); the **Detail** column points at it. What must
never happen again is an item existing in exactly one document that nobody reads.

**What belongs here:** shipped behavior that is wrong, a gap that blocks
something, a question that needs a decision. **What does not:** features and
roadmap (`IDEAS/`), settled rulings (`DECISIONS.md`), traps that are correct
behavior you must know about (`CLAUDE.md` § Live hazards), history
(git, `FJS-D675`).

**Closed items age out to [ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md).**
§ Closed below keeps the recent ones; the archive keeps the rest, verbatim.
Together they hold every id ever issued, and an id is never reused — so a
`FJS-###` named in a comment, a handoff, or a package file resolves in exactly
one of the two files. Search both before concluding an id is unknown.

## Conventions

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Id** | `FJS-###` for a defect or gap, `FJS-D##` for a decision. **Never reused, never renumbered.** Closing an item moves it to § Closed with its id. |
| **Sev** | `S1` blocker — data loss, a security hole, or cannot ship · `S2` high — silently wrong, costs a day to find · `S3` medium · `S4` low or cosmetic |
| **Status** | `open` — verified open on the date shown · `stale?` — inherited from an older audit and **not re-verified**; probe before acting · `contested` — the recorded diagnosis is doubted, see the note |
| **Verified** | The date somebody last ran it. A `stale?` row's date is when it was *written*, not confirmed. |
| **Blocked by** | A row that cannot start until another closes says `blocked by FJS-###` in its own text, and nowhere else. `fli next` takes it out of the ranking until that row closes and weighs the blocker up. Write it only where the order is real — a row that merely relates to another cites it. |
| **By hand** | A row a headless session cannot finish — a run longer than a session lasts, a check only the owner can make — says `by hand` as its own segment of its links cell. `fli next` keeps it ranked and marks it; `fix:loop` skips it. |

**A row has exactly the columns its table's header names**, and `fli
register:check` fails on anything else (`row-shape`). Both ways of getting it
wrong are silent: a row with FEWER columns is one pasted from the other table,
and the reader infers a shape from the cell count, so it is given a status
nobody wrote and no other rule can see it; a row with MORE has the excess
**dropped when the file is rendered** — in § Closed that is the *How* column, so
the row displays with no citations while they sit in the file. Links belong
inside the last declared column, joined with ` · `, and a `|` that is part of a
sentence is escaped `\|`.

`stale?` is load-bearing. The eight rows inherited from the 2026-07-31 audit
(now `IDEAS/review-coherence.md`) were re-probed on 2026-08-10 and **five of the eight were wrong**:
two were already fixed (conduit's secrets, `admin:generate`), one was never
reproducible (conduit's version skew), and two were right about a defect and
wrong about what it was — sierra's prefetch is not an auth *bypass* but a
cached 401, and caravan's row named three bugs of which two were fixed.
**Treat a `stale?` row as a lead, not a fact** (`VERIFYING.md`).

**The register also goes stale in the closing direction, which nothing here was
watching for.** `FJS-043` was fixed in the tree with a comment describing the
old defect in the past tense, and stayed `open` for eight days because closing
is a second action nobody owed. A row's `Verified` date is evidence about when
somebody last *looked*, not about whether the defect survives — 22 rows carried
`open` at 2026-08-02 when this audit ran, which is the same fiction `stale?`
exists to name, wearing the other label.

Invoice.periodEnd is a @date in the customer's zone (Lago stamps invoices.timezone). due({ by, timeZone: 'UTC' }) is empty at 2026-10-03T15:00Z, when Tokyo's grace ended, and answers at 2026-10-04T00:00Z; Los Angeles's ends 2026-10-04T07:00Z, so the same fire closes it seven hours early and the last seven hours of grace-period usage miss the invoice (they are trued up a month later). commitments({ timeZone: (tenant) => zone }) resolves per tenant DATABASE, and Lago's organizations share one, so even a per-organization zone has no spelling; due() takes one zone per call, and a sweep in Tokyo's zone is right for Tokyo and 16 hours early for LA. The workaround shipped: `closesAt DateTime @immutable`, computed at creation as startOfDay(periodEnd + graceDays, customer.timeZone), and `@@commitment(close, on: closesAt)`; SubscriptionPeriod.endsAt likewise. Its cost: the schema no longer says WHAT the deadline is, and nothing can check the instant agrees with the day and the grace (SQLite has no zones, so no @@check), pinned: a row with closesAt 2030 for a 2026 period is accepted. After one add the parent reads picked.length 0 inside the callback, and a microtask later both parent and child read 1; a second add makes both 2, so the [] reached neither side. The same parent clearing from its own button, at any other time, reaches the child (0 and 0). The kit's controls write their bound value and then call onchange in that order ([FileUpload.mesa:79](packages/ui/components/forms/FileUpload.mesa)), so a page that clears or clamps a bound value in onchange loses the write with no error: darkroom's batch emptied FileUpload's `bind:files` in onchange to keep it from listing twelve previews beside the queue, and the list stayed. | <a id="fjs-2505"></a>FJS-2505 | mesa · ui | **On the terminal target a focusable ARIA widget built from a `<div>` paints nothing and no key reaches it: `tabindex` and `role` are inert, so the kit Slider's handles are invisible and its Arrow keys unreachable** | open | 2026-10-10 | Found 2026-10-10 by the mesa-IR slice that let `on:touchstart` through, which opened `/products/`. Its price `Slider` paints only its pip numbers (`0`, `0`, `010`): each handle is an empty `<div role="slider" tabindex="0" aria-valuetext=…>`, a box with no text, and the terminal focuses only `button`, `input`, `select`, `textarea` and `<a href>`, so Tab never lands on it and `handleKeydown` never runs. A press on the handle would reach `startDrag`, whose `window.addEventListener` is a DOM read (OpenTUI's `window` shim has none). The same inertness leaves the kit's `Tab`, `DropdownItem`, `Json` and `Chart` (`tabindex=`) unreachable by keyboard. Candidates: **A** — the terminal reads `tabindex >= 0` as focusable and a widget role (`slider`, `switch`, `tab`, `option`, `menuitem`) paints what a screen reader announces, its `aria-label` and `aria-valuetext`/`aria-valuenow` (slice 28's rule for `<svg>`, extended to roles); **B** — the kit Slider moves to `<input type="range">`, and the terminal gives that a control of its own. Proof: a terminal spec that Tabs onto a slider handle, presses ArrowRight and reads the new value, and `/products/`'s frame showing `Minimum`/`Maximum` with their values. |

| <a id="fjs-2408"></a>FJS-2408 | cli | **fli next's touched term reads the last ten commits whole, so a squash-style commit marks a quarter of the register as being worked in: with two updates commits of 170 and 233 files in range, +12 fired on 163 of 625 ready rows and 26 of the top 30, and re-ranking with the working tree alone keeps 6 of those 30** | open | 2026-10-10 | Fable audit 2026-10-05, run 3.2 (2026-10-10) · [next.js](packages/cli/core/next.js) L196-205 recentPaths, git log -n10 --name-only with no per-commit cap · repro: rankNext(root, { touched: new Set(git diff --name-only HEAD) }) vs fli next --json, top-30 overlap 6 · [next.test.js](packages/cli/test/next.test.js) L104 hands touched in and never exercises the git side · +12 equals three citations and is the only term separating rank 7 from rank 300 · confirmed |
| <a id="fjs-2391"></a>FJS-2391 | ui | **On the terminal target the kit's DropdownMenu is mouse-only and closing an overlay drops focus: the menu walk and every focus restore find their element with `querySelector`, which a terminal node does not have** | open | 2026-10-10 | Found 2026-10-10 by the mesa-IR portal slice, probing the kit's DropdownMenu in the mesa terminal harness (no route that mounts one lowers yet: `/orders/:id/` stops at Tooltip's `on:mouseenter`). The menu opens under its trigger and a press on a row chooses it, but ArrowDown moves nothing (`panelEl.querySelectorAll(':is([role=menuitem]…)')` answers nothing), focus stays on the trigger, and Enter there closes the menu, so a keyboard never reaches a row. Its rows also paint side by side (`[ Edit ][ Delete ]`): they are buttons, inline in the table, and the browser stacks them by CSS the terminal does not read. `ConfirmationPopover.restoreFocus` and `DropdownMenu.closeMenu` find the trigger's control the same way, so after a close nothing holds focus and the next Tab starts from the top. The slice guarded those reads with `?.` so they no-op instead of throwing. Candidate: the items register through `$context` (the menu already hands `close` down that way) and the trigger's control is bound rather than queried, which drops the DOM query on both targets. Proof: a `verify:tui` step that opens a menu, ArrowDowns to a row and Enters it, and a Tab after a confirm's Esc that lands on its trigger. |

| <a id="fjs-2332"></a>FJS-2332 | litestone | **A @@fts(tokenize: trigram) search matches nothing for a term shorter than three characters and answers an empty list, 200, where the LIKE it replaces found hundreds** | open | 2026-10-10 | Measured 2026-10-10 in *maidtech* Q8 on production rows (account 25, 4,396 contacts), `@@fts([name, email, phone, companyName], tokenize: trigram)`: `Contact.search('jo')` and `'li'` → 0 rows; the reference's search (Prisma `contains`, LIKE) found 197 and 545 live rows. SQLite's trigram tokenizer cannot index a term under three characters, so `MATCH` answers nothing; FTS5 documents that `LIKE`/`GLOB` on a trigram table still answer one, by a scan: `contact_fts WHERE name LIKE '%jo%' OR email LIKE … ` → 233 (deleted rows included). Two letters is what a person types first: initials, a surname like Li or Ng, a state code. Nothing says the term was too short, so the empty list reads as *no such contact*. Candidates: under trigram, a term shorter than three falls back to `LIKE` over the indexed columns; at least, `search()` refuses it by name (a 400) rather than answering empty · [maidtech db/move/compare.ts](../fjs-prototypes/maidtech/db/move/compare.ts) · [maidtech PLAN.md](../fjs-prototypes/maidtech/PLAN.md) |

| <a id="fjs-2286"></a>FJS-2286 | conduit | **Conduit has no outbound pace: a target caps calls in flight but not calls a minute, per target or per credential, and the cap sheds a call rather than waiting for a slot — so a vendor's per-account rate limit is app code in every app that has one** | open | 2026-10-10 | Measured 2026-10-10, serpgrid stressor Q6. DataForSEO refuses past 2,000 calls a minute per account (dataforseo.com/help-center/rate-limits-and-request-limits), and a week's burst at Kobami's size is 34,000 calls. With conduit alone the app had two choices: max_concurrent, which bounds in-flight calls and not their rate, or its own pacer — serpgrid's pace() gives each agency an even slot of its minute, in this process only, so a second process doubles the rate. The cap also sheds: with the collector holding 8 slots, 5 of 680 scans' task_posts came back overloaded and failed, though nothing left the process; the app now waits a shed call out itself. | <a id="fjs-2050"></a>FJS-2050 | litestone | **fli explain @immutable describes only the non-sealing meaning — 'written once, at create, and never again', readOnly in the update schema — and says nothing of FJS-D167, where on a sealing model it means frozen at the seal** | open | 2026-10-08 | Found 2026-10-08, lago stressor (#7) Phase 0, by following the discovery skill's 'read the language, never your memory' rule. The entry (packages/litestone/src/core/catalog.js:505) says a column is written once at create and reaches the client as readOnly in the UPDATE schema; its see-also is 'system guarded version' and names neither sealed nor transitions. FJS-D167 rules that on a model with a @seals move the same word means frozen AT THE SEAL, moves the refusal into the WHERE, drops readOnly for x-litestone-kind 'immutable-until-seal', and survives asSystem(). Measured on a scratch schema (draft -> finalized @seals @system, total @system @immutable): asSystem() updated total in draft (ok), the move ran, the update after it was refused ('it is at finalized, which is sealed'); on a non-sealing model the same update was refused at create's rule. So the behavior is right and the description is half of it. Cost in the run: the draft schema marked Lago's long-lived draft invoice totals as 'WANTED: frozen after a STATE' and wrote them @system without @immutable, i.e. editable after finalize — the schema the explain text produced was the weaker one. Neighbors: FJS-1482 (explain has no entry for @seals), FJS-1512. |
| <a id="fjs-2049"></a>FJS-2049 | litestone | **A per-unit price finer than its currency's minor unit has no spelling that names its currency — @money is whole minor units, @money with @scale is refused, and @scale alone carries no currency** | open | 2026-10-09 | Found 2026-10-08, lago stressor (#7) Phase 0, before any app code. Lago and Stripe both price usage below a cent: $0.00025 per API call is a fortieth of a cent, and Stripe's unit_amount_decimal carries 12 places. Measured at parse (litestone parser.js, one field per probe): @money(USD) @scale(9) and @money(field: currency) @scale(6) are refused ('@money derives the scale from the currency, so state one'); @scale(12) and @scale(10) are refused (max 9); @scale(9) @big and @money(USD) @big are refused. @scale(9) alone parses, so fjs-prototypes/lago/db/schema.lite ChargeTier.perUnit and Fee.preciseAmount are bare Int @scale(9) in MAJOR units: the column says how exact it is and nothing says which currency, so formatMoney, x-money and the money-rendered-raw check all lose it. FJS-575 (closed) measured the same Lago Fee columns and deferred this as 'a separate ruling' because candidate C did not need it; a metered billing app is the caller that does. A second limit rides on it: at @scale(9) in major units a column tops out near 9,007,199.25 (2^53), so Lago's preciseAmountCents numeric(40,15) for an accumulated fee has no exact home either. Owed: a ruling on whether money can carry extra places (e.g. @money(USD, places: 9) as minor units plus n) or whether a rate is never money. · **Phase 1, 2026-10-09, lago stressor: the units are the binding ceiling, and FJS-575's premise does not hold in Lago's source.** (1) `Fee.units` at `@scale(9)` holds 9,007,199 units, which an API-call meter passes in a month; moved to `@scale(6)` (9,007,199,254). (2) units × perUnit sits at 15 places: 1,234,567 calls at $0.00025 is 308,641,750,000,000,000, past 2^53, so every intermediate is a BigInt and the toolbelt has no BigInt rounding (filed separately). (3) FJS-575 concluded a precise total is an un-rounded intermediate, never stored. Lago stores `precise_amount_cents numeric(40,15)` and READS it back: the minimum-commitment true-up sums it across the period's fees (commitments/minimum/calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:43-64), credit-note proration divides by it (credit_note_item.rb:44), and `taxes_precise_amount_cents` weights the invoice tax split (invoice.rb:669). So a running total of precise amounts exists, and at nine places it tops out near 9,007,199 of the currency · [billing.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/lago/api/test/billing.test.ts) · [rating.ts](../fjs-prototypes/lago/api/src/domain/billing/rating.ts) · Second caller 2026-10-09, serpgrid stressor (#26) Phase 0: a DataForSEO SERP task bills $0.0015 (Maps live) to $0.002 (Organic), so Scan.estimatedCost, Scan.cost, GridPoint.cost and Agency.monthlySpendCap are bare Int @scale(6) in major USD — the spend cap Q2 reconciles against the vendor's own cost names no currency · [schema.lite](../fjs-prototypes/serpgrid/db/schema.lite) · [open-questions.md](../fjs-prototypes/serpgrid/discovery/open-questions.md) |

| <a id="fjs-1879"></a>FJS-1879 | litestone | **@phone refuses letters and keeps every other spelling as typed: '-------', '(((((((' and '+0000000' are phone numbers, '(555) 123-4567' and '+15551234567' are two values, and a @@unique or a lookup keyed by a number is unique per spelling** | open | 2026-10-07 | Measured 2026-10-06 in the quo stressor, Phase 5 (Q8). Here the carrier caught it as malformed; a carrier that normalized would apply its own STOP list, and a revocation the carrier never parsed would be enforced by nobody. | <a id="fjs-1878"></a>FJS-1878 | litestone | **Consent to contact is a statement about the data, and the one word that can reach across a relation to say it, @@deny, belongs to the caller tier: asSystem() drops it, and every carrier send, automation and job writes as the system** | open | 2026-10-07 | Measured 2026-10-06 in the quo stressor, Phase 5 (Q7). A number that texted STOP may not be texted. Today that is quo's code: sendText looks for an OptOut row before it writes the outbound Message. Declared on a schema of its own, @@deny('create', direction == 'outbound' && conversation.optedOutAt != null, 'They texted STOP.') parses, reaches one hop through a to-one, refuses a member, and lets an inbound row through. asSystem() writes the same row with no refusal. In this app nobody else ever writes a Message: the browser cannot create one, a carrier webhook is a system write, and a missed-call text-back or a scheduled text is a job with no caller. FJS-D346 and FJS-D347 already name the other tier, rules graded under asSystem() because they are about the DATA (@@check, @@arc, @@exclude, @minItems). Its only open-ended word, @@check, is single-row SQL, and SQLite refuses a subquery in a CHECK. So the rule can be written, and only in the tier that skips the writer that sends. The scaffolded AGENTS.md says the schema guards every caller, including a job, a seed and a migration. For @@allow and @@deny that holds only for a job that runs on a principal's client. IDEAS/compliance-from-the-seed.md covers what an app holds, not whom it may contact. A revocation the carrier never parses (please stop texting me) is one only the app can hold, and the FCC's revocation rule requires honouring it. Wants an expression form of the data tier (an @@check that takes a litestone predicate across a to-one, graded at write like @@exclude), or a ruling that consent stays app code. The rule is also only as good as its key, which is a phone number nobody normalizes ([FJS-1879](#fjs-1879)) · [docs/access-control.md](packages/litestone/docs/access-control.md) · [inbox.ts](../fjs-prototypes/quo/api/src/domain/inbox.ts) · [consent.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/quo/api/test/consent.test.ts) · [PLAN.md](../fjs-prototypes/quo/PLAN.md) |
| <a id="fjs-1877"></a>FJS-1877 | conduit | **A target whose idempotency key is a BODY field cannot say so: the caller has to claim replayable instead of the key, conduit's own key goes in a header the target never reads, and a result never says it was a replay, so a collapsed duplicate's refusal reads as the first attempt failing** | open | 2026-10-07 | Measured 2026-10-06 in the quo stressor, Phase 5 (Q5). Telnyx Call Control collapses a repeated command_id, which is a field in the JSON body; the docs say a duplicate is ignored and do not say what it answers. TargetDescriptor.idempotency takes { header, auto } and nothing else, so quo's connector sends command_id in the body with replayable: true. That claim is false for a dial: repeating it without the key places a second call. On a sink that places the leg and loses the response (a 500), conduit replays and the carrier collapses the replay, so there is one leg. The app is answered with the replay's 422 90046 (Duplicate command_id) and gets no call_control_id. ResponseMeta has no attempt count, and onRetry is conduit-wide, not per send, so the connector cannot tell that refusal from a first-attempt one. In the ring group this rings a device the app holds no CallLeg for: the caller goes to voicemail, the answer is never bridged or hung up, and its call.answered webhook is refused 500 on every delivery. Sent instead under idempotency_key, the key goes out as an Idempotency-Key header, and two lost responses become three legs. Registering idempotency: { body: 'command_id' } is refused by name. Mutation control: removing the body key fails exactly the one-leg test. Wants the key's location to be a target fact like its header name (e.g. idempotency: { field: 'command_id' }), so the claim made is the true one and auto can mint it, plus a replay count on ResponseMeta. | <a id="fjs-1804"></a>FJS-1804 | conduit | **inbound-integrations § B's receiver record (path · verify · window · dedupe) holds none of three measured webhook dialects whole: it has no field for WHICH key verifies a delivery, none for WHOSE event it is, and its dedupe key is a header in one of the three** | open | 2026-10-11 | Measured 2026-10-06 in the quo stressor, Phase 1 (PLAN Q1). (1) Credential: Telnyx holds one PUBLIC key for every tenant, which fits a resolver-held secret. Quo signs each workspace's subscription with that subscription's own shared key, so the key is a ROW the path names, chosen BEFORE verify; conduit's ref resolver has no per-tenant credential (third-party-credentials.md leg three). (2) Owner: neither carrier names our tenant. Telnyx's is found AFTER verify from a body field that moves with the event type (the to of a text, the from of a receipt, either end of a call by direction). Quo's is fixed before verify by the path's subscription, and the body's number is looked up inside it, which is the only thing keeping one tenant's events out of another's inbox (mutation-tested). (3) Dedupe: Telnyx and Quo legacy dedupe on a body id; Standard Webhooks on the webhook-id HEADER, one per delivery, while the envelope id is per event across subscriptions. (4) Parse and dedupe read the subscription too: Quo pins a subscription's payload generation when it is created, so which envelope to expect is the row's fact, not the body's. (5) Window is a check on a SIGNED field in all three, in the dialect's unit: Quo legacy signs milliseconds. (6) Key material comes in three shapes (a 32-byte Ed25519 public key, bare base64, whsec_-prefixed base64), and Standard Webhooks' several v1 entries are the SENDER rotating, which is not the receiver-side secrets[] § What goes in toolbelt asks for. The record the three needed: path · credential(delivery) · verify · window(unit) · parse(delivery, credential) · dedupe(delivery, event, credential) · owner(event, credential) · apply, answering applied, parked or ignored · [PLAN § Phase 1](../fjs-prototypes/quo/PLAN.md) · [IDEAS/inbound-integrations.md § B](IDEAS/inbound-integrations.md) · [FJS-D177](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d177) · [quo receiver.ts](../fjs-prototypes/quo/api/src/providers/receiver.ts) · [quo doors.ts](../fjs-prototypes/quo/api/src/domain/doors.ts) · [quo.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/quo/api/test/quo.test.ts) · Two mail dialects added 2026-10-07 in the chatwoot stressor, Phase 1 (PLAN Q1). Postmark inbound: no signature at all; the credential is basic auth from the URL the account was given, so there is no signed timestamp and no window, and a captured delivery replays until the password changes; dedupe on its MessageID body field (its delivery id, not the mail's Message-ID, which is a header in Headers[]). Mailgun raw-MIME route: HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp + token and NOT the body, so a captured signature verifies over any body inside the window, which is all that bounds it; and no delivery id, since token is random per request and a retry is a new, re-signed request (modelled from Mailgun's docs in the drive's sink, not measured against live Mailgun). The dedupe key is then the mail's own Message-ID plus the envelope recipient, because one mail to two of our addresses is two deliveries with one Message-ID. Owner: neither names our tenant; the envelope recipient with its plus-tag removed is looked up as an Inbox row, the same after-verify lookup as Telnyx's number. Parse: Postmark hands over parsed JSON (it even splits the plus-tag off, MailboxHash), Mailgun raw MIME, parsed in that connector with postal-mime (inbound-email open question 3, A). So across five dialects: a credential that is a password, an HMAC over the body, an HMAC over two fields, or an Ed25519 key; a dedupe key that is a body field, a header, or the subject's own natural key · [chatwoot postmark.ts](../fjs-prototypes/chatwoot/api/src/mail/postmark.ts) · [mailgun.ts](../fjs-prototypes/chatwoot/api/src/mail/mailgun.ts) · [providers.ts](../fjs-prototypes/chatwoot/api/test/providers.ts) · Audit 2026-10-09: calendly wrote the same receiver before this row existed — [calendar-hook.ts](../fjs-prototypes/calendly/api/src/routes/calendar-hook.ts) (98 lines) + an `InboundEvent` model with `@@unique([source, nonce])` as the dedupe ([PLAN.md](../fjs-prototypes/calendly/PLAN.md) Q6, 2026-09-21); three apps now (calendly, chatwoot, quo), serpgrid Q8 is the fourth · Seen again 2026-10-09 in the serpgrid stressor, Phase 4 (PLAN Q8, Q10), two more dialects through the same hand-built record. Measured: saving the form WITHOUT touching the field leaves the row byte for byte (the form sends what changed; the drive asserts it), so nothing is corrupted silently — the field is just unusable for its one purpose. @markdown is the wrong word (the text is not Markdown and would render as it), and an app cannot target one column through registerControl because a resolver is handed the rule alone, with no model or field name. Wanted: a schema word for plain multi-line text (or code, which would reach ui's CodeInput), derived into control 'textarea'/'code' the way @markdown is. Transit leaves schemaText as it is until then; it is written by the seed and by admins through the API. · Second sighting, Transit Phase 5 (2026-10-03): Template.source holds a Mesa template, so the generated one-line box cannot edit it. Template's default form (web/src/resources/Template.mesa) is hand-written for that one column, with CodeInput, and names every field to do it. · **Code half answered 2026-10-03:** `@syntax(lang)` replaces @markdown — `x-syntax` in the JSON Schema, control `code` (CodeInput in that language) for every language but `md`, which stays a textarea. Both sightings are code, and Transit now declares them (`schemaText String @syntax(lite)`, `source String @syntax(mesa)`, and Report's `query`/`transform`/`template`): its hand-written Template form and its `registerControl` claim on `Source.schemaText` are gone, and the generated `code` control is numbered (2026-10-04, Transit `verify` green through both forms). **Still open:** plain multi-line text (an address), which is not a syntax and has no sighting yet. · blocked by `FJS-D673` |
| <a id="fjs-1656"></a>FJS-1656 | litestone | **A view's @@sql reads a @guarded column in plaintext, and an @encrypted one as ciphertext, to any caller who passes the view's gate; nothing at build says so** | open | 2026-10-03 | Found by the transit stressor (PLAN Phase 2, L9) proving sensitive fields in a landing schema held in a row. Probed 2026-10-03 with createClient({ untrusted: true, encryptionKey }) and the app's gate plugin: model Person { id String @id; score Int @guarded; email String @encrypted; @@gate("4.8.8.8"); @@allow('read', auth().isStaff) } and view personScore { id String; score Int; email String; @@sql("SELECT id, score, email FROM person"); @@gate("4"); @@allow('read', auth().isStaff) }. A level-4 staff reader gets { id } from person.findFirst() and { id, score: 7, email: 'v2.…' } from personScore.findFirst(). @guarded is documented as 'absent from reads … outside asSystem()', and FJS-D52 keeps raw SQL behind asSystem(), but a view's @@sql is raw SQL that runs for every reader the view's own gate admits, and its columns take no attributes (FJS-1643), so the protection cannot be restated on it either. Not an escalation inside one schema (whoever writes the view writes the @guarded too, and could drop it), so S3: a silent hole in what the word promises, in a trusted schema as much as a row-held one. Every client already prepares each view at build (FJS-1632); that is where a view whose result columns come from a @guarded, @secret, @hashed or @encrypted column could be refused by name, or the column marked protected on the view. Transit's landing schemas keep sensitive columns out of every view until then. |
| <a id="fjs-1655"></a>FJS-1655 | litestone | **@secret in a schema with no logger database drops its @log half without a word, and an untrusted schema can never declare one** | open | 2026-10-03 | Found by the transit stressor (PLAN Phase 2, L9), probing @encrypted/@guarded/@secret in a landing schema held in a Source row and built with createClient({ untrusted: true }). docs/encryption.md § @secret says it 'expands at parse time to @encrypted + @guarded + @log(audit). Every read and write is logged to the audit logger database.' The parser's own comment (core/parser.js, case 'secret') says '(log only if logger db declared)', and that is what happens: with no logger database the parsed field's attributes are ['secret','encrypted','guarded'] and no read or write of it is ever logged, with no warning at parse, at build or at the first read. The encryption and the guard both hold (probed: ciphertext on disk, absent from a level-4 read, refused in a where, refused on a write outside asSystem()). An untrusted schema refuses every database block by name (FJS-1633), so in a schema held in a row @secret can only ever be @encrypted @guarded spelled shorter, while its docs promise an audit trail. Either refuse @secret where no logger database is declared (naming @encrypted @guarded as the honest spelling), or let the host hand an untrusted client an audit sink it owns; and correct the docs to say which. Transit's landing schemas use @encrypted @guarded spelled out until then. |
| <a id="fjs-1648"></a>FJS-1648 | ui | **A prop a kit component does not declare lands on its root element as an HTML attribute, so <EmptyState sub="…"> renders no text and says nothing** | open | 2026-10-03 | Found 2026-10-03 (Transit). RevenueReport wrote <EmptyState title=… sub="Pick another currency…"> by analogy with SectionHeader and StatCard, which both take sub; EmptyState's body is its default slot, so sub rode {...$attributes} onto the div as sub="…" and the sentence never rendered, through a browser drive that asserted the title. Nothing warned: not the compiler, not fli check, not the browser. A lowercase name that is not a known HTML/ARIA attribute or data-*, passed to a kit component that declares no such prop, is almost always a misremembered prop. Wants a compile-time or dev warning naming the component's props, or a fli check rule over kit components' declared exports. |
| <a id="fjs-1645"></a>FJS-1645 | litestone | **loadRows holds every record of its source in memory before writing, so a 200,000-row CSV of 12.6 MB peaks at 1.4 GB RSS: about 110 times the file** | open | 2026-10-03 | Measured in the transit stressor, 2026-10-03 (PLAN M1), the day loadRows landed: orders.csv (5,000 rows) 206 ms / 125 MB peak RSS into :memory:, 237 ms / 128 MB into a file; orders-wide.csv (200,000 rows) 4.85 s / 1.39 GB into :memory:, 4.97 s / 1.41 GB into a file. The landing target costs nothing (file vs memory within 3%); the memory is loadRows reading the whole CSV into records, then a second array of coerced rows, before the first batch is written. Phase 2's REST source arrives page by page and wants the same shape. |

| <a id="fjs-1624"></a>FJS-1624 | ui | **An editable <Json> always keeps its own undo stack — ⌘Z bound on its root, ↶/↷ buttons in its corner — and takes no way to hand history to the page, so a tree that is one editor among several over the same document is a second stack beside the page's** | open | 2026-10-02 | Found 2026-10-02, *dragonfly, the JSON-grid stressor*, Phase 2 (PLAN.md Q2). [Json.mesa](packages/ui/components/display/Json.mesa) under `editable` keeps `past`/`future` (HISTORY = 50), renders the two history buttons whenever `canEdit`, and `onGridKey` calls `onHistoryKey` for every keydown on the tree, with `preventDefault` and no opt-out. Its own comment says the binding is to the TREE so a page with its own history keeps the shortcut, but a page that owns history needs the shortcut INSIDE the tree too: dragonfly opens a <Json editable> in a grid cell beside a JSON text box, and both write one document. ⌘Z in the tree undoes the tree's last edit and announces it through `onchange` as a new write, which the page's stack records as one more step; the page's ⌘Z then lands in the tree as `somebody else's edit`, which the tree's `remember(draft)` pushes onto its own `past` — so each stack can undo the other's undo, and the ↶ in the cell walks a history that does not match the page's. Asked for: `history={false}` (no stack, no buttons, no key binding; every write still announced), so the caller's stack is the only one · [Json.mesa](packages/ui/components/display/Json.mesa) · **Measured** 2026-10-02 in dragonfly, Chrome 150 over CDP, a <Json editable> open in a grid cell beside the page's own history (which takes ⌘Z in the capture phase, so the tree's binding never sees it). The filed mechanism was a guess, and half of it is wrong; what happens is this. (1) Edit city to `Austin TX` in the tree, press the TREE's ↶: the city goes back, and the page records that as a new write. The page's Undo then puts `Austin TX` back — it undoes the tree's undo — and a second page Undo is needed to take the edit away: two presses for one edit, the first going the wrong way. (2) Edit, then page ⌘Z: the city goes back, and the tree's ↶ stays enabled; pressing it announces the document the page already holds, changes nothing, and disables itself — a dead press. The tree's `$: value` handler drops its draft when the announced document comes back, so a value arriving from outside is not pushed onto `past` here; the page's restore is invisible to the tree's stack, which is why (2) is a dead press and not a redo. Both are the same defect: two stacks over one document, and the caller cannot turn the tree's off. |

| <a id="fjs-1566"></a>FJS-1566 | portal | **Portal, the search stressor: a page that leaves <head> unclosed is captured as ok with 0 words, because the reader counts head as a skipped element and HTMLRewriter never ends it before <body>, so the whole body is skipped** | open | 2026-09-29 | Found seeding the knight persona (2026-09-29). https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/ opens <head>, then <meta>/<link>/<script>, then <body> with no </head> (valid HTML: the end tag is optional, and <body> implies it). parsePage on the fetched 44 KB answered 0 words; the same page from <body> on, or the <article> alone, answered 4,080. Both readers share the shape: SKIP lists head and counts depth by skip++ / e.onEndTag(skip--), so an implied end never lowers it. Text: [parse.ts:131](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/parse.ts) (SKIP at :64); copy: [article.ts:107](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/article.ts) (SKIP at :28). The Page is written status ok, text and html null, words 0, so Read later opens an empty copy, the library search never finds the page, and nothing on the page says the capture failed. A fixed parser will not reach these rows by itself: capture.ts:71 counts words != null as having a copy, so a link check never recaptures a 0-word page; staleParses (reparse from snapshot) would, if PARSER is bumped. Fix: treat <body> (or the first body-only element) as the end of head, or drop head from SKIP and skip only its children (title, meta, link, script, style are already skipped or empty) |

| <a id="fjs-1466"></a>FJS-1466 | litestone · junction | **`@@fts` has no way to say *match without the marks*. None of its tokenizers folds Greek accents or Hebrew points, and `tokenize:` takes a name and nothing else. So the fold is app code on both sides, a loader that writes a shadow column and a service that folds the query, and the declared `$search` directive, which does neither, answers `βίβλος` as typed with 0 rows.** | open | 2026-09-28 | **Measured** 2026-09-28, *remnant, the legacy-port stressor*, Q3, on the real corpus (31,100 verses, 443,808 words). **Every existing route, one at a time:** (1) the four tokenizers: 0 of 6 probe words (`γενεσεως βιβλος Ιησου בראשית ברא אלהים`) against the text as written. Under the default `unicode61`, Hebrew points are separators, so `בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית` indexes as the fragments `ב`, `אש`, `ית`. (2) A tokenizer argument: `tokenize: "unicode61 remove_diacritics 2"` is refused at parse (`Expected IDENT`), and it would not help: over NFD text in plain FTS5 it folds 2 of 6, because FTS5's diacritic table stops at U+0331, so the perispomeni (U+0342), the iota subscript (U+0345) and every Hebrew point and accent (U+0591–U+05C7) survive. (3) **The nearest declaration that exists**: `function fold(s: String): String { @@expr("replace(…)") }` plus `textFolded String @fold(text)`. It takes 199 nested `replace()`s (the 147 precomposed letters and 52 marks this corpus holds, 3.7 KB of SQL), and it agrees with the JS fold on all 443,808 words and hits 6 of 6. But it writes in 24.1 s against 8.8 s for a JS-folded column (9.0 s for `@@fts` over the raw text), it is keyed to this dataset's characters (a data release bringing one more is silently unfolded), and the query side still needs a JS twin: a schema function is inlined into DDL, not a callable SQL function, and bun:sqlite registers none. **What remnant shipped** ([fold.ts](../fjs-prototypes/remnant/api/src/core/fold.ts): NFD, strip `\p{M}`, drop transliteration's syllable dots): five shadow columns written by the loader, and the query folded in [search.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/remnant/api/src/services/search.service.ts). Over HTTP every probe and all four of Q3's queries (`G0976`, `βίβλος`, `biblos`, `record`) find Matthew 1:1, median 1–8 ms. **What it costs:** nothing ties the shadow to its source, so a write of `text` that forgets `textFolded` leaves the index answering the old text. Adding it to a loaded corpus took a 46 s refold through the client, because SQL cannot compute the fold, while the same fold at load time is free. And **every other entrance misses**: `GET /api/verses?$search=βίβλος` → 0 rows, `biblos` → 0, and only a pre-folded `βιβλος` → Matthew 1:1. **And it is not only accents**: the corpus writes ί as U+1F77 in all 2,138 lemmas that carry it, while a Greek keyboard types U+03AF, which is canonically the same letter in different bytes. So an unnormalized index misses even a correctly accented query. **Candidate**: a word on the index, `@@fts([text], fold: marks)` (NFD, strip marks), with litestone keeping the shadow on every client write, as it already stamps `@default(ulid())` in JS, and folding the query inside `search()`. Then `$search`, a Resource's search and a console all agree. Measured for Greek and Hebrew only; by FTS5's own table the same holds for any mark above U+0331 (read, not measured) · [remnant PLAN.md Q3](../fjs-prototypes/remnant/PLAN.md) · [remnant search.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/remnant/api/test/search.test.ts) |

| <a id="fjs-1438"></a>FJS-1438 | litestone | **`@@allow('update', …)` grades the row BEFORE the write, so a move of a foreign key into somebody else's parent is admitted unless the model also declares `'post-update'` — an operation the catalog does not list. *Portal, the search stressor* had the hole twice: its new Bookmark filed into a friend's collection, and its Phase 1 DomainRule moved into a friend's SHARED lens, where his grantees' searches read it** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Measured** 2026-09-28 in *Portal, the search stressor* (PLAN.md § Bookmarks), at the litestone layer and again over HTTP. `@@allow('create', collectionId == null \|\| collection.ownerId == auth().id)` refuses a create into Joe's collection; the same predicate in `@@allow('update', ownerId == auth().id && (…))` admitted `PATCH collectionId → Joe's` (200, stored), because `update` compiles to a WHERE over the row as it IS. | <a id="fjs-1318"></a>FJS-1318 | ui | **`CommandPalette` cannot show a server's search results: it takes no query callback, and it ranks whatever `items` it is given against the typed words AGAIN, so a hit made on text the row does not show is dropped and the person reads *No results*.** | open | 2026-09-23 | **Driven in a real browser**, linear Phase 6 (Chrome, `vite dev`). linear's ⌘K is fed by `GET /api/search` ([search.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/linear/api/src/services/search.service.ts): FTS5 over issues, comments and projects, graded per model). The palette then passes those items through `rank(items, query, { keys: ['label', 'group', 'sub'] })` and draws only what that keeps. **Measured:** *throttling*, a word in ENG-3's description: the server answered **1** hit (`Rate-limit the search endpoint`), and the palette drew **0 rows**, *No results for "throttling"*. *flamingo* (inside a comment's first 80 characters) and *load-test* (in a title) drew 2 and 1, because the word happens to be in the label. | <a id="fjs-1271"></a>FJS-1271 | litestone | **A `File` ref stores the origin it was uploaded against, so every stored file points at the old host the moment an app moves — and the key that would survive the move is sitting in the same JSON.** | open | 2026-09-22 | **Measured** while moving `example`'s drives off the dev ports. The ref in `product_image.file` is `{"key":"storage/ProductImage/2e6246fc4edd.png","provider":"local","endpoint":null,"publicBase":"http://localhost:8110",…}` — the key is relative and portable, and `publicBase` beside it is not. Start the same app on another port and every photograph 404s or refuses the connection while the bytes sit untouched under `storage/`; the drive that found it read `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:8110` from a browser whose API was answering on 7110. **A port is the cheap version of the real case, which is a DOMAIN**: an app that moves from `shop.example.com` to its own domain, or gets a CDN in front of storage, orphans every uploaded file in every row, and no migration can be written for it without parsing JSON in SQL. **Nothing reports it** — the rows read fine, the API answers, and only a browser fetching the url finds out. **What it costs today**: `example`'s drives cannot move the API port, which is why they move only the dev server. **The likely answer is that `publicBase` is DERIVED at read time** from the provider's current config plus `key`, which is § V.5 exactly — a stored copy of something the config already knows. Against it: an object genuinely served from a URL the current config no longer describes, which is an argument for keeping `endpoint` per row and not for keeping the app's own public base. **The derived path already exists and the stored value shadows it**: `urlFor` is *if a publicBase was stored in the ref, use it* ([storage/index.js:44](packages/litestone/src/storage/index.js)) and falls back to `endpoint` + `key` only when the ref carries none, so the smallest change is which of the two wins. It is written at upload in [file.js:234](packages/litestone/src/storage/file-storage.js). Needs a ruling before a change · found by `verify:cart` and `verify:catalog` · blocked by `FJS-D875` |
| <a id="fjs-1269"></a>FJS-1269 | notifications | **Nothing in the framework can reach a phone, and the stated reason for building it here — *a subscription is a row* — is the one thing an app already gets for free. The reason to build it is the 350 lines of RFC that every app otherwise writes identically and gets silently wrong.** | open | 2026-09-22 | Q5 of the connectteam stressor, answered ([PLAN.md § Q5](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/PLAN.md)). The brief refuses both shipped transports in one sentence — *if the reminder is an email nobody opens, or a badge inside an app that is not running, the person is late and we have paid for a system that did nothing* — so this product is the first on the list that is WRONG rather than lesser without push. **Ground state re-probed 2026-09-22:** `ls packages/notifications/drivers/` is `email.ts`, `inapp.ts`; `grep -rn 'vapid\|web-push' packages/ --include=*.ts --include=*.js` is **0 hits across the whole framework**. **What was free, and it is worth saying first.** The `transports:` seam cost nothing: anything with `send(recipient, message, app)` registers, a registered driver beats a built-in name, a transport with no driver is refused BEFORE any delivery rather than at the moment one is needed, and a `push:` formatter beside `inApp:` on a `defineNotification` needs no adapter. Nothing in the app is a workaround for this package. **What 2.17 and `ecosystem-gaps.md` § 16 both get wrong.** Both argue that making the subscription a Model *is the whole argument for building it here rather than leaving it to an app*, because it then inherits `@@gate`, `@encrypted` on the keys and Invariant 7's redaction, where *every hand-rolled version is a plain table with none of that*. **Measured: a hand-rolled version in a FrontierJS app is not a plain table.** `model PushSubscription` was declared in the app's own `db/schema.lite` and got all three — `@encrypted` hides `p256dh`/`authSecret` from every caller read and returns PLAINTEXT to `asSystem()`, which is what a sender needs and is the one of the five visibility words that fits; the audit trail carries `[redacted]` (see [FJS-1266](#fjs-1266) for the half of that which is a defect); and the gate is the app's to state. That argument is an argument for litestone, which the app already has. **What actually costs, measured.** `api/src/core/push.ts` is **~350 lines** implementing RFC 8291 (aes128gcm over ECDH-ES), RFC 8188 (the body framing) and RFC 8292 (VAPID): an ephemeral P-256 keypair per send, **four HKDF derivations** whose `info` strings must be byte-exact including their NULs, a `salt‖rs‖idlen‖keyid` header, the `0x02` last-record delimiter, and a JWT whose signature must be raw `r‖s` where node emits ASN.1 DER by default. **Every one of those fails the same way: the push service does not hold the key, cannot tell a bad derivation from a good one, and answers `201 Created`.** A wrong build is indistinguishable from a phone in a tunnel, which is why the app's own test decrypts what it encrypts with a device private key rather than asserting a length — every cheaper check passes on garbage. **Three more things an app must build that the driver interface does not suggest.** (1) **A driver that WRITES**: a subscription expires with no notice and the only signal is a 404/410 on a send, so the transport that delivers is the one that must prune; `transport`/`send`/`shutdown` hints at none of it. (2) **A fan-out inside the fan-out**: `inApp` writes one row per recipient, but a person is N devices with N key pairs and N independent 410s, and `Recipient` — whose design note is *a Recipient is not a User* — has nowhere to put them. (3) **`asSystem()` on every send**, because the keys are `@encrypted` and the sender reads everybody's rows, which is [FJS-1216](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1216)'s cost once more: every delivery is filed against the application rather than against anybody. **The boundary § 16 says to settle first, with a measurement.** *A push payload is a read that leaves the building via a vendor, so `@guarded` columns must not be in it.* It cannot be enforced at the driver: the driver necessarily holds `asSystem()` to decrypt the subscription keys at all, so it has full visibility by construction. The check belongs where the payload is BUILT — the notification's `push:` formatter — or nowhere. **Scope note:** measured to the edge, no vendor send, per that run's scope call. The request is built completely — URL, headers, VAPID JWT, encrypted body — and handed to an injected `deliver`; the default is a plain `fetch`, since a push service is ordinary HTTPS with no SDK and no account, which is what makes this buildable by an app at all. · `IDEAS/overview.md` 2.17 · `IDEAS/ecosystem-gaps.md` § 16 · [FJS-1270](#fjs-1270) · [FJS-1266](#fjs-1266) · [FJS-1234](#fjs-1234) · driven in `api/test/reminders.test.ts` |
| <a id="fjs-1266"></a>FJS-1266 | litestone | **An `@encrypted` column reaches the audit trail two different ways depending on WHO wrote the row — `[redacted]` for a system write and ABSENT for everybody else's — so a trail reader cannot tell *the column was not supplied* from *it was supplied and you may not see it*.** | open | 2026-09-22 | Found on connectteam Phase 6 ([PLAN.md § Q5](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/PLAN.md)) and driven as a pair: two creates of one model with identical data, one through `asSystem()` and one as the ordinary USER(4) caller who owns the row. `model PushSubscription` declares `p256dh String @encrypted`, `authSecret String @encrypted` and `@@log(audit)`. The system write's `after` carries `"p256dh":"[redacted]"` and `"authSecret":"[redacted]"` — **Invariant 7, exactly as promised**. The owner's write has neither key in `after` at all. The trail is built from the row as the WRITER could read it back, and the visibility table's `@encrypted` row is *caller writes, caller does not read* — so for every principal below the system client the column is not redacted, it is missing. **Not a nulls-are-dropped artefact:** `userAgent`, a plain nullable column the same caller left unset, is in the same snapshot as `null`. The consequence is that the one question a trail exists to answer about a credential column — *was a device key written, or rotated, here* — has no answer. Absent means *not supplied* on the system path and *supplied, hidden* on every other, with nothing in the row to separate them, and a reader has no way to know which path wrote a given row. Invariant 7's promise is that such a column *logs as `[redacted]`*, which is a claim about presence as much as about the value. **What would close it:** build the snapshot from the row as WRITTEN and then redact, rather than from the row as read back. The redaction already exists and is already applied on the system path — this is which value it is applied to. · driven in `api/test/reminders.test.ts` § 3 · [FJS-D349](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d349) is the other direction of the same trail (a log that reveals too much) |
| <a id="fjs-1254"></a>FJS-1254 | sierra | **A `type` declared in `db/schema.lite` reaches the browser's own schema registry and the UI realm cannot address it: a Resource naming one silently renders the form for the SERVICE'S model instead — a different field list, and nothing warns.** | open | 2026-09-22 | **Driven in a browser**, connectteam Phase 5. Every write in this app that matters is a custom method whose payload is not a row of any model: `shifts.assign` takes `type AssignShift` (the trio a manager types, who, where and an availability override) because the model's two instants are `@system` and three overlap rules run on the way in. No warning from the resource, none from `<Form>`, and `fli check` green — `resource-model-miss` fires on a name that resolves to nothing, not on one that resolves to something else. **So the declaration a custom method is validated against on the server is invisible to the screen that fills it in**, and the labels, required flags and option lists get written out by hand in the page — the exact second copy the framework's one rule exists to prevent. Junction already takes `methods: [{ method: 'assign', input: 'AssignShift' }]` and validates the body against it (measured: a bad `onDate` comes back `400 [{ field, message }]`, rendered under the control), so the two ends of the same declaration disagree only about the browser. Either a Resource should be able to name a `type` and generate from it, or naming one should be refused by name · [schedule/index.mesa](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/web/src/routes/schedule/index.mesa) · [schema.lite § What a screen sends that is not a row](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/db/schema.lite) |

| <a id="fjs-1242"></a>FJS-1242 | cli | **`fli check` runs its rules over a schema litestone itself refuses to parse and exits 0 — so `bun run check` is green on a schema that cannot migrate and kills the app at boot.** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Measured** in the connectteam stressor on one line — `kioskPin String @hashed @guarded` on a model, which litestone refuses with *@hashed conflicts with @guarded*. Against that file: `litestone validate` errors, `litestone migrate create` refuses, and the app's own boot throws (`_buildEnv`, `testing.js:141`). `fli check` prints `⚠ 31 rule(s) checked · 9 warning(s)` and **exits 0**, saying nothing — it reads the schema well enough to run `transition-methods` over every move in it. `fli check --list` holds 61 rules and none asserts that the schema parses: `schema-in-memory` grades whether the committed artefacts describe the running models, which is a different question and passes here. **The only thing that failed `bun run check` was the scaffold's generated `api/test/access.test.ts`**, which calls `parse()` for its own reasons; with that one file replaced by a trivial passing test, the whole gate exits 0 — 31 rules, lint clean, typecheck clean, 1 pass. Every scaffold's `AGENTS.md` names `fli check` as the Data-realm gate and `bun run check` as *the same gate CI runs*, and the generated `ci.yml` runs only that. Same family as [FJS-1228](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1228) — the gate does not read the UI realm either — one realm over, and this is the realm `fli check` exists for. **A second instance, a different class of error and a worse ending.** `@@gate("4.6.5.6")` violates the ladder's non-decreasing rule. Parse does not catch it — the gate is validated at plugin init — so `litestone migrate create` wrote a migration and `fli db:migrate` **applied it**, creating 23 tables for a schema `createClient` then refuses with *levels must be non-decreasing in R.C.U.D order*. `litestone validate` catches it and exits 1, because it is the one tool that runs both passes; `fli check` exits 0 again. So the honest statement of this row is not *`fli check` misses one rule* but **there is no single command in the gate that answers "will this schema run"** — and the one that does (`litestone validate`) is not in `bun run check`, not in the generated `ci.yml`, and is named in no scaffold's `AGENTS.md`. Adding it to the `check` script is a one-line fix. Found by the connectteam stressor, `fjs-prototypes/connectteam/PLAN.md` Phase 1. **Third instance, 2026-09-27, *Portal, the search stressor* Phase 1** — a third class: `@@unique([ownerId, lensId, domain])` over an optional `lensId`, which litestone refuses as *cannot be enforced* (and names the fix). `fli check` exits 0 (33 rules, 2 warnings); `fli advise` and `createClient` refuse; `bun run check` went red only through the scaffold's `access.test.ts` calling `makeTestClient` — the same single thread. **And the one-line fix this row proposes is the wrong line, measured:** `litestone validate` is *which STORED rows this schema would now refuse* — it opens `db/app.db`, so on a schema ahead of the database (every change before its migration) it exits 1 with *no such table* per new model, and with no `app.db` (CI; it is gitignored) it creates an empty one and exits 0. The command that answers *will this schema run* without a database is `fli advise`: exit 1 on the refusal above, exit 0 on the fixed schema with warnings. The second is every app scaffolded before 2026-10-08 16:23: `bun run check` stays green until the migrate · [lago PLAN.md § Phase 1](../fjs-prototypes/lago/PLAN.md) · Audit 2026-10-09: Charter hit it on hosted apps — a schema `fli check` passes and the app does not boot ([PLAN.md](../fjs-prototypes/charter/PLAN.md)); chatwoot's [FJS-1936](#fjs-1936) is the same shape for `createClient` |

| <a id="fjs-1230"></a>FJS-1230 | ui | **`slot="name"` is honoured by exactly one component in the kit and silently dropped by every other — so a `<Card>` given a header and a footer renders neither, and the screen looks finished rather than broken.** | open | 2026-09-21 | Found when a user of the calendly stressor reported a dead end on the Availability screen. The real damage was one layer past it: **that page had lost both of its headings AND both of its forms**, and nothing anywhere said so — no warning, no console message, no build error. The add-window form and the add-exception form simply were not in the DOM, so the screen read as an empty state that had been designed. [Card.mesa](packages/ui/components/layout/Card.mesa) declares `header` and `footer` as snippet props and renders `{@render header?.()}`; **it references `$slots` zero times**, so `<h2 slot="header">` and `<div slot="footer">` are dropped. [Form.mesa:928-932](packages/ui/components/forms/Form.mesa) does both — `{@render actions?.()}` `{:else if $slots.actions}<slot:actions />` — and is **the only component in `packages/ui/components` that does**; measured across every component declaring a snippet prop, `Form` is 1 and all the rest are 0. **The kit already knows this is a real trap, and fixed it in one direction only.** Form's own comment: *Two spellings because two protocols reach a component and the rest of this kit uses the other one: every other container here (Card, Table, EmptyState, SectionHeader) takes its trailing content as a snippet prop, so a caller who wrote `{#snippet actions()}` over a form got no buttons and no complaint.* That is this bug with the operands swapped, it was worth a code change when it pointed at Form, and the general case was left open. **Apps are actively taught the dropped spelling.** Every Resource `fli scaffold` generates ends with `<Button slot="actions" …>` inside a `<Form>` — correct, because Form is the exception — so a developer reads `slot=` as the kit's idiom and writes `<h2 slot="header">` on the next Card they reach for. That is exactly the path this app took. **This is [FJS-1208](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1208)'s class met a second time**: content handed to a component and discarded with no diagnostic. That one was `<EmptyState>` dropping children across 28 call sites in basecamp; this one is every container in the kit dropping named slots. The narrow fix is the `$slots` fallback Form already has, copied to Card, Table, EmptyState and SectionHeader. **The better fix is the one neither has: warn.** A component that receives `$slots.<name>` it will not render knows, at render time, that it is throwing content away — and a `console.warn` naming the component and the slot would have turned a silent blank screen into a one-line answer. Nothing else catches it: `fli check` (34 rules) and `fli typecheck` are both green over the broken page, and Biome cannot read `.mesa` at all ([FJS-1228](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1228)) · [Card.mesa](packages/ui/components/layout/Card.mesa) · [Form.mesa:928](packages/ui/components/forms/Form.mesa) · [FJS-1208](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1208) · the stressor's `web/src/routes/availability/index.mesa` · blocked by `FJS-D668` |

| <a id="fjs-1246"></a>FJS-1246 | example | **`example`'s payroll has no input shape for a MEASURED hour: `annualGross` is `rate * hoursPerWeek * 52` and `hoursPerWeek` is an `Int` contracted constant, so a workforce product's whole output can reach a payslip only by being averaged back into the contract it was measured to replace.** | open | 2026-09-22 | **Graded, not ported** — PLAN.md § Q6 in the connectteam stressor, against the shapes `example/api/src/domain/payroll/` demands and with nothing copied into that tree. An approved timesheet (`@@transitions`, `@seals`, lines carrying `onDate`, `kind`, `minutes` and a `rateSnapshot` frozen at the rate in force on the day) was converted into `PayWindowRow` and run through transcribed copies of `annualGross` and `periodShare`. **It goes, and everything that makes it a measurement is lost on the way.** Spring fortnight: 420 measured minutes, **€84.00 actually earned**, → `{ basis: 'hourly', rate: 1200, hoursPerWeek: 4 }` → `annualGross` €2496.00 → `periodShare(·, 26)` **€96.00 — out by €12.00**. Autumn fortnight: 540 minutes, €108.00 earned → `hoursPerWeek: 5` → €3120.00 → **€120.00, out by €12.00**. **Four refusals, and only the fourth is one a type checker catches.** (1) `hoursPerWeek` is an `Int @gte(0) @lte(168)`, so a fortnight holding one 7-hour night is **3.5 h/week and is stored as 4** — the rounding alone is the whole €12.00. (2) `PayWindow` holds ONE `rate` for a window while a timesheet holds a `rateSnapshot` per LINE, so a raise mid-period is a fact about a day at one end and a fact about a window at the other, and neither shape can express the other without losing the split. (3) `PayComponentKind.overtime` is in `EARNING_KINDS` and `draftPayslip` emits exactly one earning line, always `basicPay`; `overtime` is reachable only through `arrears.ts`, which is a CORRECTION to a previous period — so a timesheet that HAD overtime lines would have nowhere to put them. The record's own observation (*an enum value nothing in the application produces*) measured from the other side, and the timesheet builder cannot produce one either, because overtime is a rule about a WEEK and no row in either schema holds one. (4) `employeeId: number` against a uuid. **The loop is therefore not closable at this joint**, and the reason is a modelling one rather than a bug: `example` prices a CONTRACT and a workforce product establishes a MEASUREMENT, and the only bridge available re-derives the contract from the measurement and then pays the contract. Whether the fix is a third basis (`measured`, whose lines ARE the gross), or a `Payslip` that can be drafted from lines rather than from a window, is the open question. Nothing here is a defect in what `example` ships — it is the input shape being the one thing that was taken on faith · [employment.ts § annualGross](example/api/src/domain/payroll/employment.ts) · [payslip.ts § draftPayslip](example/api/src/domain/payroll/payslip.ts) · [handoff.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/src/domain/payroll/handoff.ts) · [hours.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/test/hours.test.ts) |
| <a id="fjs-1214"></a>FJS-1214 | litestone | **[`FJS-D143`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d143) ruled on 2026-08-25 that a column declares what KIND of time it holds, and nothing implements it — so the first product that needs a recurring wall-clock time cannot spell its central object.** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Measured**: `grep -rn "timeZone\|timezone" packages/litestone/src --include=*.js` → **0 hits**, no `zoned`, no `wallClock`, and no import of `@frontierjs/toolbelt/datetime`. The catalog's only time words are validators — `@date`, `@datetime`, `@time`, all in the *Refuse a bad value* group — so *Tuesdays 09:00–17:00 in Europe/Lisbon* is stored as `String @time` with the zone in a sibling column on another model and the relationship between them held by a comment. **Corrected 2026-09-20 after measuring the browser payload — the gap is narrower and sharper than first filed.** The FORMAT half already works end to end: `@time` crosses as a `pattern` plus `x-time`, and sierra's control resolver renders `<input type="time">` for it, in a branch whose own comment reads *a wall clock has no zone, so `<input type="time">` round-trips it and the plain input is right* ([field-rules.js:619](packages/sierra/src/resource/field-rules.js)). So the framework already holds the wall-clock CONCEPT in three places — that resolver, toolbelt's `fromWall`/`resolveWall`, and `FJS-D143` itself — and the schema language is the one place that cannot say it. What is missing is the ZONE BINDING: nothing declares that this column resolves against `schedule.timeZone`, so the pairing is convention held by a service that remembers, no query can ask *is this instant inside this window* (the zone resolution SQLite cannot do is the same one `FJS-D143` measured as a silent NULL), and the comparison lives in application JS — where this app has already written it wrong once, applying its time check to one branch of a two-branch function. **The arithmetic is not what is missing** — `@frontierjs/toolbelt/datetime` already exports `fromWall`, `resolveWall`, `partsIn` and `plainDateIn` with Temporal's `disambiguation` vocabulary, which is the twenty lines the ruling scoped. What is missing is the declaration that binds a column to a zone, and a comparison the framework computes and binds. A plain DATE has the same gap wearing the other half of the vocabulary (`AvailabilityOverride.date`, *not the 24th*), so one word plausibly carries both. Found building the calendly stressor, where it is the reason the exercise was chosen · [`IDEAS/time-and-recurrence.md`](IDEAS/time-and-recurrence.md) · [catalog.snapshot.md](packages/litestone/catalog.snapshot.md) · [datetime.js](packages/toolbelt/src/datetime/datetime.js) · [schema.lite § AvailabilityRule](../fjs-prototypes/calendly/db/schema.lite) **Priced in the connectteam stressor, 2026-09-22 — the answer is money, in both directions, and the two errors cancel.** *Tuesdays 22:00–06:00, Europe/Lisbon* at €12.00/h, driven across both of Lisbon's 2026 boundaries. The wall clock the manager typed is **480 minutes on every night of the year**, because it cannot see a boundary. The night starting Sat 28 March is **420 minutes** (`2026-03-28T22:00Z` → `2026-03-29T05:00Z`, offset 0 → +60); the night starting Sat 24 October is **540** (`2026-10-24T21:00Z` → `2026-10-25T06:00Z`, offset +60 → 0). So the same rota line pays **€96.00 both nights against €84.00 and €108.00 actually worked — overpaid €12.00 in spring, underpaid €12.00 in autumn**. **The two errors cancel over a year, which is what makes this worse than a one-directional bug**: an annual total reconciles, a year-on-year comparison reconciles, and nothing audits to anything. One person, one weekly night shift, on a rota of sixty. **The layer that should have owned the difference is the COLUMN.** `startLocal String @time` says it holds a time and not which zone reads it, so the app resolves the instant pair itself and stores it in two `@system` columns — and **nothing in the language knows those two columns were derived**. Measured: a depot entered as `Europe/Lisbon` that is really in the Azores, corrected afterwards to `Atlantic/Azores`, leaves every stored `startsAt` **one hour out, permanently, with nothing anywhere disagreeing** — and because both zones observe DST the error is CONSTANT rather than seasonal, so even the comparison that would have caught the DST version cannot see it. **And the validator half is missing too, which is how the wrong zone got in.** `Site.timeZone String @default("UTC")` accepted `"banana"` without complaint and threw at the first shift, from `@frontierjs/toolbelt/datetime` — one layer below the one that should have refused the write. The IANA set is knowable at parse time (`Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone')`), so `@zone` is a validator that could exist beside `@date`, `@datetime` and `@time` and does not. | <a id="fjs-2321"></a>FJS-2321 | litestone | **The wasm engine names every cell through sqlite3_column_name, and the browser worker opens two connections per device file with a 32 MB page cache each** | open | 2026-10-10 | Found by the 2026-10-09 performance audit (B4, B5). B4: rows are built by a per-cell sqlite3_column_name call across the wasm boundary, 20,000 name decodes for a 2,000 × 10 result that produce the same 10 strings; read the names once per prepared statement and build rows in a loop of one shape. B5: databases.js opens a writer and a reader per file, each at cache_size = -32768, in a single-threaded worker: 64 MB of wasm heap allowance on a phone, and every write invalidates the reader's cache anyway. When the engine declares a single connection, reuse the writer as the reader the way :memory: already does, with a cache nearer 4 MB · [sqlite-wasm.js](packages/litestone/src/engines/sqlite-wasm.js) · [databases.js](packages/litestone/src/core/databases.js) |

| <a id="fjs-2287"></a>FJS-2287 | caravan | **unique holds while a job runs, so a one-per-key worker cannot queue its own successor: work that must run until its key is drained is one long-lived handler, and the moment between its last read and its end needs a cron watcher to catch the dispatch the lock refused** | open | 2026-10-10 | Measured 2026-10-10, serpgrid stressor Q6: one DataForSEO collector per agency (the vendor's limit is per account), dispatched under unique: scan-collect:<agencyId>. | <a id="fjs-2280"></a>FJS-2280 | example | **`/cart/` lists ✓ in `fli dev:tui` and throws `location is not defined` when opened: the route reads the widget handoff off `location.hash` and erases it with `history.replaceState`, the address the router owns** | open | 2026-10-09 | Found 2026-10-09 by the mesa-IR router slice, which let routes importing `page` open (`FJS-2271`). `src/stores/cart.js` `handoffCodeFromUrl()` and `routes/cart/index.mesa:90` reach the browser's globals; the terminal has the router's memory History and no `location`, and `--list` grades lowering, which is compile-only. Two fixes, one a ruling: `page` carries the fragment (it holds `pathname` and `search` and not `hash`) and the route clears it with `goto(..., { replace: true })`, or the app is told a DOM global in a route is web-only. | <a id="fjs-2267"></a>FJS-2267 | litestone | **`loadMigrationSql` caches a file's SQL by `mtimeMs`, so a migration file rewritten within one mtime tick of its last load reads back as the OLD text — a BLOCKED section deleted by the reviewer is still refused in that process** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Measured** 2026-10-09: `test/migrations-fixes.test.ts` *a file holding a BLOCKED section runs nothing and records nothing* fails about one run in two, alone or in the suite — `again.refused` is `true` after the BLOCKED lines were stripped. UserDaily declares crew Crew? @relation(fields: [crewId]) and crewDay CrewDaily? @relation(fields: [crewId, day], references: [crewId, day]); both share crewId. Creating a UserDaily whose (crewId, day) has no CrewDaily is refused — right — but the message attributes the composite's columns to the single-column relation that shares its first field, so it sends the reader to a Crew that is there. The DDL is correct (FOREIGN KEY (crewId, day) REFERENCES crew_daily (crewId, day)); include works both ways. Wants: the refusal names the relation whose fields match, crewDay → CrewDaily · [client.js](packages/litestone/src/core/client.js) · [ela PLAN Q4](../fjs-prototypes/ela/PLAN.md) · Seen again in the data move: `sys.userDaily.create({ data: { crewId: 1, day } })` with no CrewDaily → "crewId,day … names no Crew (relation crew)" · Found by the ela data move (Phase 3) · [PLAN.md](../fjs-prototypes/ela/PLAN.md) · Seen again 2026-10-08, ela Phase 6: a missing CrewDaily reported as 'names no Crew' while seeding survey scores |

| <a id="fjs-1567"></a>FJS-1567 | portal | **Portal, the search stressor: page capture does not follow a <meta http-equiv=refresh> redirect, and a capture that reads 0 words is still status ok, so a redirect stub or a client-rendered page is kept as an empty copy with nothing to say so** | open | 2026-09-29 | Found seeding the knight persona (2026-09-29). https://www.conventionalcommits.org/ answers 200 with a 208-byte page whose only content is a meta refresh to /en/; https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/ answers 200 with 152 bytes refreshing to /essay/local-first. [fetch.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/fetch.ts) follows HTTP redirects only (redirect: 'manual', each hop re-checked by the SSRF guard), and nothing in api/src/domain/pages reads a refresh. Both were kept as status ok, words 0, finalUrl the stub. A client-rendered page does the same: https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/ (content in a <template>, filled by script) is ok with 0 words; not a parser defect, but indistinguishable from one on the page. [capture.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/src/domain/pages/capture.ts) writes status ok for any parse, and capture.ts:71 (hasCopy = words != null) then treats the empty copy as kept, so a link check never retries it. Fix: follow a same-document meta refresh (delay 0, http(s) only) as one more guarded hop; and write a 0-word parse as failed (for example 'the page had no readable text'), keeping link live, so the page shows the capture failed and offers Capture again. Seen with FJS-1566, whose empty copies are the same symptom from a different cause |

Today the nearest thing is accidental: `fli dev` prefixes come from bun run --parallel ([new.md:265](packages/cli/commands/project/new.md#L265)), which colors by script ORDER, so dev:web is yellow in one app and cyan in the next. **Where it would help:** (1) fli dev log prefixes and its banner (slot · web 8003 · API 8103), each surface and port in its color; (2) every realm-tagged log line -- litestone, caravan, junction $.log -- so a scrolling terminal sorts itself; (3) fli ci phases, fli proves / prove, fli check findings, fli next and fli ws:atlas, tagged by realm or surface; (4) fli new and fli make:* output naming what they created; (5) a FrameworkError's terminal print naming the realm it was thrown in; (6) the browser tab in dev -- a tinted favicon per surface so web and site tabs differ, the Sierra error overlay border, the dev banner; (7) Litestone Studio chrome in the Data color, Junction devtools in API, each registerDevService entry in its own; (8) the VS Code extension -- file icons for .lite (Data) and .mesa (UI), folder colors for api/ web/ site/ db/, the status bar; in @frontierjs/css it is a tone for DEV chrome only and never reaches a shipped app's styling (Invariant 13); color is never the only signal -- a label or glyph goes with it, NO_COLOR and 16-color terminals degrade cleanly, and the palette is checked for color-blind separation; "surface" already means a background layer in @frontierjs/css (surface.css), so the naming must not add a third sense. **Open questions (decision-rules):** realm as hue family and surface as a shade inside it (web, site, widgets, extension and desktop are all UI) or a distinct hue per surface; what color cli gets; whether Deployment and Testing get colors or stay neutral |

| <a id="fjs-1256"></a>FJS-1256 | junction | **A custom method has ONE answer, and it is both the caller's result and the payload broadcast to every other tab — so a write whose useful answer is a report makes every connected client log *ignored an update with no id* and drop it.** | open | 2026-10-09 | **Driven in a browser**, connectteam Phase 5. `timesheets.build` writes a `Timesheet` and one `TimesheetLine` per measured clock entry, and what the caller needs back is the report — how many lines, which clocks were still running, which days had no pay rate — so it answers `{ sheet, lines, stillRunning, noRate }`. That answer is announced on the service's channel under the method's own name, and junction's client logged `[Junction] ignored an update with no id — it cannot be matched to a row. An announcement carries the record it is about.` The documented instrument is `$.dispatch = false`, which is a boolean: the app can announce a shape no client can use, or announce nothing and leave every other tab unaware that a timesheet now exists. There is no third spelling — `$.dispatch` cannot name the row to announce, and returning the row instead loses the report the caller came for. The row's own guidance names the read-shaped case (*a count, a report, a credential* → `$.dispatch = false`); this is the write-shaped one, where silence has a cost. A `$.announce(row)` beside `$.dispatch`, or a method-level `announces:` naming which part of the answer is the record, would close it · [timesheets.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/connectteam/api/src/services/timesheets.service.ts) · Seen again 2026-10-09 in the serpgrid stressor, Phase 4: clients.provision answers an outcome ({ outcome, clientId, locationId }), and driven in Chrome every open tab was refused it as a Client ('every one of 2 subscribers was refused a clients broadcast') until the method said $.dispatch = false by hand · [serpgrid clients.service.ts](../fjs-prototypes/serpgrid/api/src/services/clients.service.ts) |
